report:
**Conclusion:** Your view is supported by the best available evidence: induced abortion has **not** been shown to increase breast-cancer risk.

**Why the claim persists:** Some older *retrospective case–control* studies found an association. These ask women with and without cancer to report prior abortions. Because abortion can be underreported—and women with cancer may disclose it differently—this design is vulnerable to **recall/reporting bias**. It also can inadequately account for reproductive factors that affect breast-cancer risk, such as age at first full-term birth.

**Stronger evidence:** A major collaborative Lancet reanalysis of 53 studies (83,000 women with breast cancer) found that studies using abortion information recorded *before* cancer diagnosis did not show increased risk (reported relative risk for induced abortion: 0.93). The researchers concluded that the positive findings from retrospectively collected histories were likely misleading because of differential disclosure. A later systematic review/meta-analysis focused on prospective studies likewise evaluated the question using the less bias-prone design.

The American Cancer Society’s current summary is consistent: the most up-to-date research indicates abortion does not affect a woman’s breast-cancer risk. Thus, an individual observational study that reports an association is not, by itself, evidence that abortion causes cancer—especially when the association disappears in prospective-record studies.

Sources:  
- https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html  
- https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(04)15835-2/fulltext  
- https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10552-015-0536-1
